### Rule 125 : Icon column alignment

> A row-level state (running, queued, failed, ...) is the activity column
> below, and `internal/app/activity_guard_test.go` enforces it (A-16,
> DEVDESK-143).

**Any icon column (or icon + short text) must be left-aligned.**

Nerd Font icons have variable width depending on the terminal. Left alignment is the only one that guarantees consistent rendering.

| Content type | Alignment |
|-----------------|------------|
| Icon alone | **Left** |
| Icon + short text | **Left** |
| Alphanumeric text | Left (default) |

#### An icon in the first column **is** a column

When a `datatable`'s first column carries a glyph, it is a column in its own
right — not a prefix stuck onto the neighboring text cell.

| | |
|---|---|
| Title | **empty**. The glyph reads in a glance; a header would be naming something that does not need naming, and `eza` does not put one there either. |
| Width | `datatable.IconColumnWidth` (2): the glyph, plus one cell so it does not touch the text. Two, not one — a Nerd Font glyph renders double-width on some terminals, and a single cell would truncate it there. |
| `Sizing` | `SizingFixed`. Nothing to measure. |
| `Less` / `Search` | **none**. It adds no text anyone could type, so filtering stays on the name columns; and a comparator would cost two more cells to fit its sort arrow. |

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the glyph has its own column
{
    Title: "", Sizing: datatable.SizingFixed, MinWidth: datatable.IconColumnWidth,
    Cell: func(r row) string { return r.icon() },
},
{
    Title: "Name", Sizing: datatable.SizingContent, MinWidth: 16,
    Cell:   func(r row) string { return r.Name },
    Search: func(r row) string { return r.Name },
},

// ❌ WRONG — the glyph stuck into the identifying column
{
    Title: "Name", Sizing: datatable.SizingContent, MinWidth: 18,
    Cell: func(r row) string { return theme.IconDocker + " " + r.Name },
},
```

**What sticking it in costs**, and this is what settles it: the identifying
column spends its width on something that is not the name, and a
`SizingContent` then measures the glyph along with it — so the table's most
contested column reserves two cells for an icon, at every width.

#### An icon's color goes through a **role**, never through the glyph

Rule 122 applies here as everywhere: `Cell` renders the bare glyph, `Style`
colors it. What Rule 125 adds is **where the color comes from** —
`theme.IconStyle(role)`, and a role declared in `theme/iconcolors.go`.

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the view names a meaning, the theme answers with a color
Cell:  func(r row) string { return nodeKindIcon(r.node) },
Style: func(r row) lipgloss.Style { return theme.IconStyle(nodeKindRole(r.node)) },

// ❌ WRONG — the view decides the hue
Style: func(r row) lipgloss.Style {
    return lipgloss.NewStyle().Foreground(theme.ColorSecondary)
},
```

**A codepoint is not a name.** A table of `U+F0849 → ColorSecondary` cannot
be reviewed: nothing on the line says whether the entry is correct, so an
error there is indistinguishable from a deliberate choice. A role can be
discussed, which is why it is the key.

The roles are overridable via a theme file (`icon_namespace`,
`icon_repository`, `icon_vis_*`, `icon_image`, `icon_container`; `IconRoleContainer`
is the resting icon of a running container, `ColorText` by default) — unlike syntax colors, which are closed
aliases: an icon is the first thing seen on a row, so it is the part of the
palette a user is most likely to have an opinion about.

**All three icon tables declare a `Style`** — `ws`, `:sec`, and the
explorer — and a fourth that did not declare one would be the application's
only monochrome icon column. A missing role shows: the cell falls back to
`ColorText` (see `IconColor`), so an oversight renders ordinary text rather
than nothing.

**The same object keeps its color from one view to another.** A git repo is
`IconRoleRepository` in `ws`, in `:sec`, and in the explorer — the role is
shared, not duplicated. This is the property for which the key is a meaning
rather than a glyph: the three views do not even show the same glyph for it.

**The granularity is that of the action, not that of the type.** `ws`
colors in three classes — repo, directory, file — which are exactly the
three branches of `availability.go`, and **not** a shade per language the
way `eza` does: `.go` versus `.rs` changes no shortcut on the row, so the
color would say nothing. An icon column is colored by what the row lets you
do.

**The color disappears under the cursor**, like that of any colored column:
the selected row is rendered whole by `styles.Selected` (Rule 122). An icon
column therefore cannot be the *only* carrier of a piece of information —
which is why the explorer's kind stays readable another way (the glyph
outside selection, the position in the tree inside it).

The three tables concerned are `ws`, `containers`, and the `:sec` inventory,
and they declare the same constant. `TestAnIconColumnIsUntitledAndTwoCellsWide`
(`internal/ui/datatable`) scans the sources and rejects a titleless column
that invents its own width. It does not see the other half — a glyph stuck
into a text cell is indistinguishable from a name that starts with a
glyph — which stays a matter for review.

#### The activity column

**In a view with long-running operations (jobs, agents, containers), the first
column is the activity indicator.** It is built by `datatable.IndicatorColumn`,
never by a literal `Column` with an `Indicator` field set (`TestOnlyIndicatorColumnSetsIndicator`
rejects it). It keeps the icon-column shape above: untitled, `SizingFixed`,
`datatable.IconColumnWidth`. When the row is at rest (`indicator.Idle`) the
cell shows the row's own icon via its `theme.IconStyle` role, or an empty cell.

- **The color says the state, never the operation.** A scan, a clone and a
  `docker stop` that are running all look the same: `●` / `○`. What is being
  done is the footer's and the Jobs view's business.
- **No green for "done".** `Done` is `◉` in `ColorActivityNeutral`. Green stays
  reserved for the exceptions Rule 122 lists.
- **The colors are closed aliases**, assigned in `ApplyTheme`:
  `ColorActivityRunning`, `ColorActivityNeutral`, `ColorActivitySuspended`,
  `ColorActivityFailed`. They are not `icon_*` roles and no theme file gains a
  key: a theme that retuned them per state would break the one alphabet of

- **The glyph carries the meaning, the color repeats it.** Under the cursor
  the color is repainted on `ColorTableLineSelected` and the glyph still reads.
- **The blink phase is read at render.** The router's `jobs.FrameMsg` carries
  it; the view calls `m.table.SetBlinkPhase(msg.Blink)` and nothing is rebuilt.
  Without the call the phase is on: a running row shows a steady `●`. A view
  starts no timer of its own for a row (`app.motion: static` pins it on).
- **Guarded.** `internal/app/activity_guard_test.go` (A-16, DEVDESK-143) fails

  a migrated package that holds `AdvanceSpinner`, `StatusColumn:`, a `Frame`

Forbidden:
- ❌ A literal `Column{Indicator: …}` instead of `datatable.IndicatorColumn`
- ❌ A glyph literal (`"●"`, `"⊗"`) in a view: use `indicator.Glyph`
- ❌ A color chosen in the view for an activity state
- ❌ Green for a finished operation
- ❌ A color that depends on the type of operation

Forbidden:
- ❌ `.Align(lipgloss.Center)` on an icon column
- ❌ `.Align(lipgloss.Right)` on an icon column
- ❌ A title above a glyph column
- ❌ A local width (`colIconFixed`, `statusColumnWidth`, a literal `2`) instead of `datatable.IconColumnWidth`
- ❌ A glyph prefixed inside a text column's cell
- ❌ An icon color chosen in the view instead of a `theme.IconStyle` role
- ❌ A color table indexed by the glyph rather than by meaning
- ❌ An icon column with no `Style`, while the other three have one
- ❌ A role per file type where the row offers the same actions

### Rule 139 : A `datatable`'s body is never replaced — not by a loading screen, not by a message

**A `datatable` stays a table, whatever it contains.** Whether it is
loading its data, empty because nothing has run yet, or empty because a
filter no longer matches anything, the rendered body is always
`m.table.View()` — header included, no rows. `datatable.View()` already
does this on its own: a zero-element table renders its header and fills
the rest with the background (`internal/ui/datatable/render.go`). Nothing
in a view therefore needs to detect this case.

What a body would have said instead — loading, the row count, a verdict —
is **the footer's and header's business**, never the body's:

- loading is a `components.Status{Text: "...", Activity: true}` in the
  footer, the shared dot, for a view's own load and for work the router
  tracks (Rule 128). That mark is for the *table's data*
  loading; an operation on one row is the row's activity dot (Rule 125),
  never a loading body;
- the row count, or whatever stands in for it (a verdict, a total), is a
  field of `GetHeaderInfo` (`shortcut.HeaderInfo{Key: "Images", Value: "0"}`) —
  it, not the body, answers "what am I looking at."

**Why.** A body that substitutes itself for the table — with a loading screen or
with text — loses its header and its columns for as long as the condition
holds, then regains them: the layout jumps on every refresh, every
`ctrl+r`, every keystroke in the filter. The header and the footer, on the
other hand, have a fixed height (Rule 124): what they display changes
without ever moving the table.

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the body is always the table; the footer and header speak
func (m Model) renderImagesView() string {
    return m.imageTable.View()
}

func (m Model) status() sharedcomponents.Status {
    if text, ok := m.loadingLabel(); ok {
        return sharedcomponents.Status{Text: text, Activity: true}
    }
    return sharedcomponents.Status{Text: m.actionLine()}
}

func (m Model) GetHeaderInfo(_ string) []shortcut.HeaderInfo {
    return []shortcut.HeaderInfo{
        {Key: "Images", Value: fmt.Sprintf("%d", len(m.imageTable.Visible())), Style: theme.HeaderValueStyle},
    }
}

// ❌ WRONG — the body replaces itself with a loading screen

    return theme.DimStyle.Render("Loading images...")
}

// ❌ WRONG — the body replaces itself with a message, empty or filtered
if len(m.imageTable.Visible()) == 0 {
    return theme.DimStyle.Render("No images found")
}
```

The blink phase is pushed from the `jobs.FrameMsg` handler:
`m.footer.SetBlinkPhase(msg.Blink)`, and the view implements `WantsBlink()`
(return `status().Activity`); without them the dot is steady on. The braille
spinner is removed: no file under `internal/` imports
`charm.land/bubbles/v2/spinner` (`TestNoViewImportsTheBubblesSpinner`).

`TestNoTableViewRendersALoadingBody` (`internal/ui/components`) rejects a
loading body in table views, with no declared exception.

**Declared exception: a welcome screen, not a status message.** The empty
`:sec` inventory (`internal/ui/security/inventory.go`, `renderEmptyInventory`)
replaces the body with a paragraph that explains *where scans come from* —
this is not "0 rows," it is first-use onboarding, with more content than a
header field can carry. The distinction: a message that fits in
`GetHeaderInfo` (a count, a status) goes there; text that explains an
entire application flow stays an explicit exception, like the one already
provided for loading.

### Rule 136 : Filter Bar for Tables

**Every table view must use `components.FilterBar` for search and toggle filters. No ad-hoc filter implementations.**

#### Behaviour

| State | Bar visible | Description |
|-------|-------------|-------------|
| No filter | ❌ | Bar is completely hidden |
| Toggle filter active | ✅ | Bar shows dimmed placeholder + active token(s) |
| Search mode (after `/`) | ✅ | Bar shows focused text input + active token(s) |
| Search confirmed (query set) | ✅ | Bar shows dimmed placeholder + query token + toggle tokens |

#### Visual

The filter bar forms a **closed rectangle** that visually connects with the viewport's bottom border:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐   ← viewport top border
│  table rows...                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤   ← viewport last line, joined (= rectangle top)
│  / cursor...         [tcp]  ·  [LISTEN] │   ← content line with │ sides
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘   ← rectangle bottom border
```

Both lines use `theme.ColorViewportBorder` for `│`, `└`, `┘`, `─` characters.
The viewport's last line is `└───┘` when no bar is shown and becomes `├───┤`
when one is.

**The router detects the bar from the shape of the footer's first line
(`components.OpensWithBarFrame`); no view declares it.** A footer only starts
with a `│…│` line through `components.BarFrame`: a view that draws its own
`│…│` first line would make the router join the viewport to it, so never do.

#### Placement — Footer, not viewport

The filter bar is rendered in `RenderFooter()`, **not** in the viewport content.

- `GetFooterHeight()` returns `baseFooterHeight + filterBar.ExtraHeight()`
- `RenderFooter()` prepends `filterBar.View()` when `filterBar.IsVisible()`
- Table height formula does **not** subtract `filterBar.ExtraHeight()` — the app router handles that via `GetFooterHeight()`

#### Integration Pattern

```go
// In Model struct
filterBar components.FilterBar  // or components.NewFilterBarWithTokens(tokens)

// In GetFooterHeight()
func (m Model) GetFooterHeight() int {
    return 2 + m.filterBar.ExtraHeight() // base (empty line + info) + filter bar
}

// In RenderFooter()
func (m Model) RenderFooter(width int) string {
    var parts []string
    if m.filterBar.IsVisible() {
        parts = append(parts, m.filterBar.View())
    }
    parts = append(parts, theme.EmptyLineBg(width), infoLine)
    return strings.Join(parts, "\n")
}

// In resize() / WindowSizeMsg handler — NO ExtraHeight subtraction
tableHeight := m.height - overhead  // overhead = header row only, NOT filterBar.ExtraHeight()
m.table.SetHeight(tableHeight)

// In Update() / key handler — forward keys when in search mode
if m.filterBar.InEditMode() {
    m.filterBar, cmd = m.filterBar.Update(msg)
    m.applyFilters()
    return m, cmd
}
// "/" key activates search
case "/":
    return m, m.filterBar.ActivateSearch()

// In InEditMode() — propagate to app router
func (m Model) InEditMode() bool {
    return m.filterBar.InEditMode() || /* other edit states */
}

// In View() / renderNormalView() — table only, NO filter bar here
func (m Model) renderNormalView() string {
    return m.table.View()
}

// In applyFilters() — use filterBar.SearchQuery() for text filtering
query := strings.ToLower(m.filterBar.SearchQuery())
```

#### Toggle filter tokens (views with dedicated filter keys)

Use `components.NewFilterBarWithTokens()` and update token active state when toggle keys are pressed:

```go
// Init
fb := components.NewFilterBarWithTokens([]components.FilterToken{
    {Label: "tcp"},
    {Label: "udp"},
})

// On key "t"
fb.SetTokenActive("tcp", !fb.IsTokenActive("tcp"))
```

#### Rules

- ✅ Use `components.FilterBar` — never re-implement the filter bar locally
- ✅ The frame itself is `components.BarFrame(width, inner)`: that is what
  `FilterBar.View()` calls, and the only path for whatever shares this slot
  without being a filter — the viewer's go-to-line prompt (§3.53). Two
  implementations of the rectangle would be free to diverge on where the
  corners sit.
- ✅ Only one occupant of the slot at a time, and the height does not depend
  on which one — otherwise the panel resizes under the reader whenever one
  opens on top of the other.
- ✅ `filterBar.ExtraHeight()` must be added to `GetFooterHeight()` return value
- ✅ `filterBar.View()` must be prepended in `RenderFooter()` when `filterBar.IsVisible()`
- ✅ `filterBar.InEditMode()` must propagate via the view's `InEditMode()` method
- ✅ `"/"` key must always call `filterBar.ActivateSearch()`
- ❌ Filter bar must NOT be rendered inside the viewport (`View()` / `renderNormalView()`)
- ❌ `filterBar.ExtraHeight()` must NOT be subtracted from table height (app router handles it)
- ❌ `filterInput textinput.Model` fields in view models (use FilterBar instead)

## Code quality rules and proactive checks

### Rule 301 : Systematic code quality check before commit

**MANDATORY**: Before creating a commit, ALWAYS perform the following checks:

#### 1. Go linter (golangci-lint)
```bash
golangci-lint run
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Fix ALL warnings and errors
- ✅ Specifically check deprecation warnings (SA1019)
- ✅ NEVER ignore warnings without documented justification

#### 2. Tests
```bash
go test ./...
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Verify that all tests pass
- ✅ If tests fail, fix them BEFORE the commit

#### 3. Build
```bash
go build
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Verify that the build succeeds without errors
- ✅ Test the application if functional changes were made

#### 4. Deprecated dependencies

**Detection:**
- Check golangci-lint SA1019 warnings
- Look in go.mod for packages marked as deprecated

**Action:**
- Replace IMMEDIATELY with a maintained alternative
- Document the replacement in the commit message
- Update the documentation (.claude/CLAUDE.md)

**Examples of common replacements:**
- `github.com/go-ping/ping` → `github.com/prometheus-community/pro-bing`

### Rule 302 : IDE diagnostics check

**MANDATORY**: Before each commit, check the IDE diagnostics:

```
Use mcp__ide__getDiagnostics to check:
- Compilation errors
- Unused parameters
- Unused imports
- Other warnings
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Fix or justify every diagnostic
- ✅ Do not ignore "unused parameter" without a reason

### Rule 303 : go.mod and dependencies

**After any dependency change:**

```bash
go mod tidy
go mod verify
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Verify that go.mod is up to date
- ✅ Verify that go.sum is consistent
- ✅ Document new dependencies in .claude/CLAUDE.md

### Rule 304 : Quality commit message

**Mandatory format for quality fixes — in English (see Rule 307):**

```
type: short description

Detailed description explaining:
- What was detected (warning, error, etc.)
- Why it was a problem
- How it was resolved

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

**Commit types for quality:**
- `fix:` - Bug fix detected by linter
- `chore:` - Deprecated dependency replacement
- `refactor:` - Code quality improvement

### Rule 305 : MANDATORY pre-commit checklist

**Before EVERY commit, check:**

- [ ] `golangci-lint run` → 0 warnings
- [ ] `go test ./...` → PASS
- [ ] `go build` → SUCCESS
- [ ] `mcp__ide__getDiagnostics` → No critical error
- [ ] `go.mod` up to date (if dependencies changed)
- [ ] Documentation updated (if API changed)
- [ ] Tests added (if new feature)

**If EVEN ONE of these checks fails:**
- ❌ DO NOT create the commit
- ✅ Fix it first
- ✅ Restart the checklist

### Rule 306 : MANDATORY proactivity

**Claude Code MUST:**
- ✅ Check the linter WITHOUT the user asking
- ✅ Propose fixes BEFORE the commit
- ✅ Flag deprecated dependencies AS SOON AS they are detected
- ✅ Document all quality changes

**Claude Code MUST NEVER:**
- ❌ Wait for the user to flag a warning
- ❌ Create a commit with unresolved warnings
- ❌ Ignore dependency issues
- ❌ Forget to update the documentation

### Correct workflow examples

**Example 1 - Feature commit:**
```
1. Write the code
2. go build → verify compilation
3. golangci-lint run → fix warnings
4. go test ./... → verify tests
5. mcp__ide__getDiagnostics → check the IDE
6. git commit with a detailed message
```

**Example 2 - Detecting a deprecated dependency:**
```
1. golangci-lint detects SA1019
2. Look up the recommended alternative
3. Replace the import and the code
4. go mod tidy
5. Test that everything works
6. Update .claude/CLAUDE.md
7. git commit explaining the replacement
```

### Rule 307 : Commits and code comments — English only

**Every git commit message and every comment in the code must be written
in English**, regardless of the language used to converse with the user.

| Element | Language |
|---------|--------|
| Commit message (title + body) | ✅ English only |
| Code comment (`//`, `/* */`, docstring) | ✅ English only |

## Code editing instructions

### Rule 201 : Code must be clean, concise, and well-structured to stay maintainable

#### Extracting functions from Update()
- **Strict limit**: If a case in `Update(msg tea.Msg)` exceeds **5 lines**, extract it into a separate function
- **Naming**: `handle[MessageType]` (e.g. `handleContextSwitch()`, `handleKeyPress()`)
- **Pattern**: The function must return `(tea.Model, tea.Cmd)`

**Before (bad):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
```

**After (good):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    return a.handleContextSwitch(msg)

// Further down in the file
func (a *App) handleContextSwitch(msg ContextSwitchCompleteMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
}
```

#### Code reuse
- **Zero duplication**: If a block of code appears 2+ times, create a function
- **Modules**: Group related functions together (e.g. all context switching in a single file)
- **Constants**: Extract magic values into named constants

#### Error handling
- **Bubble Tea pattern**: Errors = messages (e.g. `ContextSwitchErrorMsg`)
- **Always log** in DEBUG mode: `log.Printf("ERROR: %v", err)`
- **Never ignore**: If the error is non-critical, document why

#### Comments
- **Mandatory for**:
  - Exported (public) functions
  - Complex business logic
  - Workarounds or non-obvious decisions
- **Format**: `// functionName does X and returns Y`
- **Avoid**: Comments that repeat the code

#### Complexity
- **Maximum 3 levels of indentation** in a function
- **Functions > 50 lines**: refactor into smaller functions
- **Switch > 10 cases**: consider a table-driven pattern

154	// ThemeDir returns the themes directory (~/.devdesk/themes/)
155	func ThemeDir() (string, error) {
156		homeDir, err := os.UserHomeDir()
157		if err != nil {
158			return "", err
159		}
160		return filepath.Join(homeDir, ".devdesk", "themes"), nil
161	}

163	// LoadTheme loads a theme from a JSON file.
164	// If name is empty, "dark" or "default", returns the built-in default theme
165	func LoadTheme(name string) (*Theme, error) {
166		if name == "" || name == "dark" || name == "default" {
167			return DefaultTheme(), nil
168		}
169	
170		data, err := readThemeFile(name)
171		if err != nil {
172			return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to read theme '%s': %w", name, err)
173		}
174	
175		var t Theme
176		if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &t); err != nil {
177			return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to parse theme '%s': %w", name, err)
178		}
179	
180		if err := validateTheme(&t); err != nil {
181			return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid theme '%s': %w", name, err)
182		}
183	
184		// Ensure the name is set
185		if t.Name == "" {
186			t.Name = name
187		}
188	
189		return &t, nil
190	}

192	// readThemeFile returns the bytes of <name>.json: the user's copy in
193	// ~/.devdesk/themes first, then the one embedded in the binary. A name that is
194	// in neither gives an error wrapping fs.ErrNotExist.
195	func readThemeFile(name string) ([]byte, error) {
196		file := name + ".json"
197		if dir, err := ThemeDir(); err == nil {
198			data, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, file))
199			if err == nil || !errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist) {
200				return data, err
201			}
202		}
203		return themes.FS.ReadFile(file)
204	}

206	// ListThemes returns the list of available themes: "default" (built-in) first,
207	// then the union of the shipped themes and the JSON files in the themes
208	// directory, sorted, without duplicates.
209	func ListThemes() ([]string, error) {
210		seen := map[string]bool{"default": true}
211		var names []string
212		add := func(entries []fs.DirEntry) {
213			for _, entry := range entries {
214				if entry.IsDir() {
215					continue
216				}
217				if themeName, ok := strings.CutSuffix(entry.Name(), ".json"); ok && !seen[themeName] {
218					seen[themeName] = true
219					names = append(names, themeName)
220				}
221			}
222		}
223		if dir, err := ThemeDir(); err == nil {
224			if entries, err := os.ReadDir(dir); err == nil {
225				add(entries)
226			}
227		}
228		if entries, err := themes.FS.ReadDir("."); err == nil {
229			add(entries)
230		}
231		sort.Strings(names)
232		return append([]string{"default"}, names...), nil
233	}

235	// hexColorPattern is the only colour form a theme file may hold.
236	var hexColorPattern = regexp.MustCompile(`^#([0-9a-fA-F]{3}|[0-9a-fA-F]{6})$`)
237	
238	// validateTheme treats every string field of Theme other than name as a colour
239	// (a new non-colour string field must be excluded here). It refuses a theme
240	// holding a non-empty colour that is not #rgb or #rrggbb, naming the first
241	// such key (in declaration order) and its value. An empty value is not an error:
242	// it selects the fallback applyColor documents.
243	func validateTheme(t *Theme) error {
244		v := reflect.ValueOf(t).Elem()
245		for i := 0; i < v.NumField(); i++ {
246			key, _, _ := strings.Cut(v.Type().Field(i).Tag.Get("json"), ",")
247			if key == "name" || v.Field(i).Kind() != reflect.String {
248				continue
249			}
250			if val := v.Field(i).String(); val != "" && !hexColorPattern.MatchString(val) {
251				return fmt.Errorf("%s: %q is not #rgb or #rrggbb", key, val)
252			}
253		}
254		return nil
255	}

257	// applyColor returns a color.Color from a hex string, or the fallback if empty.
258	func applyColor(hex string, fallback color.Color) color.Color {
259		if hex == "" {
260			return fallback
261		}
262		return lipgloss.Color(hex)
263	}
264	
265	// Hex formats c as "#rrggbb". Anything that is not a color.RGBA (NoColor, the
266	// empty Color, an ANSI index, nil) has no fixed value and gives "none".
267	func Hex(c color.Color) string {
268		rgb, err := rgb8(c, "hex")
269		if err != nil {
270			return "none"
271		}
272		return fmt.Sprintf("#%02x%02x%02x", rgb[0], rgb[1], rgb[2])
273	}

275	// ApplyTheme applies a theme by updating the global color variables
276	// then refreshing all styles
277	func ApplyTheme(t *Theme) {
278		// Update the global semantic colors
279		ColorOK = lipgloss.Color(t.ColorOK)
280		ColorError = lipgloss.Color(t.ColorError)
281		ColorWarn = lipgloss.Color(t.ColorWarn)
282	
283		ColorPrimary = lipgloss.Color(t.ColorPrimary)
284		ColorSecondary = lipgloss.Color(t.ColorSecondary)
285		ColorBorder = lipgloss.Color(t.ColorBorder)
286		ColorText = lipgloss.Color(t.ColorText)
287		ColorDim = lipgloss.Color(t.ColorDim)
288		ColorHighlight = lipgloss.Color(t.ColorHighlight)
289		ColorWhite = lipgloss.Color(t.ColorWhite)
290		ColorBlack = lipgloss.Color(t.ColorBlack)
291		ColorBackground = applyColor(t.ColorBackground, ColorBackground)
292	
293		// Apply per-component colors (falling back to semantic colors)
294		ColorTitleFg = applyColor(t.TitleFg, ColorPrimary)
295		ColorAppTitleFg = applyColor(t.AppTitleFg, ColorPrimary)
296		ColorSubTitleFg = applyColor(t.SubTitleFg, ColorSecondary)
297	
298		ColorButtonFg = applyColor(t.ButtonFg, ColorWhite)
299		ColorButtonBg = applyColor(t.ButtonBg, ColorPrimary)
300		ColorButtonInactiveFg = applyColor(t.ButtonInactiveFg, ColorWhite)
301		ColorButtonInactiveBg = applyColor(t.ButtonInactiveBg, ColorDim)
302	
303		ColorTabActiveFg = applyColor(t.TabActiveFg, ColorBlack)
304		ColorTabActiveBg = applyColor(t.TabActiveBg, ColorSecondary)
305		ColorTabInactiveFg = applyColor(t.TabInactiveFg, ColorDim)
306		ColorTabInactiveBg = applyColor(t.TabInactiveBg, ColorCmdLineBg)
307	
308		ColorTableHeaderFg = applyColor(t.TableHeaderFg, ColorSecondary)
309	
310		ColorCmdLineFg = applyColor(t.CmdLineFg, ColorHighlight)
311		ColorCmdLineBg = applyColor(t.CmdLineBg, ColorCmdLineBg)
312	
313		// Falls back to ColorCmdLineBg: assigned after ColorCmdLineBg above rather
314		// than beside the other Table* colors, since a fallback read before
315		// ColorCmdLineBg's own assignment this pass would see last theme's value
316		// instead of this one's, the same ordering ColorChartBg below depends on.
317		// Any theme file predating this key omits it, so this fallback is what most
318		// installs actually render with.
319		ColorTableLineSelected = applyColor(t.TableLineSelected, ColorCmdLineBg)
320	
321		// A chart's background is that of the command line: it's the surface
322		// "one shade lighter" that every theme already defines, so a chart
323		// stands out from the rest of its box without any theme having to
324		// declare one more color.
325		ColorChartBg = ColorCmdLineBg
326		ColorCmdLineInactiveFg = applyColor(t.CmdLineInactiveFg, ColorDim)
327	
328		ColorViewportBorder = applyColor(t.ViewportBorder, ColorBorder)
329	
330		ColorHeaderKey = ColorSecondary
331	
332		// Syntax colors: aliases of the semantic palette, assigned here rather than
333		// at declaration because the palette itself is only populated by this
334		// function — a package-level `= ColorSecondary` would capture the zero
335		// value and never follow a theme change. ColorChartBg above is the same
336		// pattern.
337		ColorSyntaxKey = ColorSecondary
338		ColorSyntaxString = ColorOK
339		ColorSyntaxNumber = ColorHighlight
340		ColorSyntaxLiteral = ColorPrimary
341		ColorSyntaxPunct = ColorDim
342		ColorSyntaxTag = ColorSecondary
343		ColorSyntaxAttr = ColorPrimary
344		ColorSyntaxComment = ColorDim
345	
346		// A keyword shares the literal's colour today, and that is deliberate
347		// rather than an oversight: `if` and `true` are both words of the language,
348		// so the pairing is defensible until a theme decides otherwise — at which
349		// point it has a name to decide about. It is the argument already made for
350		// ColorFooterError against ColorError.
351		ColorSyntaxKeyword = ColorPrimary
352	
353		// A heading takes the key colour, and its weight comes from the style
354		// rather than from here.
355		ColorSyntaxHeading = ColorSecondary
356	
357		ColorSearchMatch = ColorHighlight
358		ColorSearchMatchFg = ColorBlack
359	
360		// Severity colors (background + foreground pairs)
361		ColorSeverityCritical = applyColor(t.SeverityCritical, ColorError)
362		ColorSeverityCriticalFg = applyColor(t.SeverityCriticalFg, ColorBlack)
363		ColorSeverityHigh = applyColor(t.SeverityHigh, ColorSeverityHigh)
364		ColorSeverityHighFg = applyColor(t.SeverityHighFg, ColorBlack)
365		ColorSeverityMedium = applyColor(t.SeverityMedium, ColorWarn)
366		ColorSeverityMediumFg = applyColor(t.SeverityMediumFg, ColorBlack)
367		// A theme that omits the two LOW keys gets ColorDim under ColorBackground,
368		// the pair the shipped dark themes set (D181). ColorDim is held to 4.5:1 on
369		// the background on every theme, so the pair reads on dark and light alike.
370		// Both fallbacks read ColorDim and ColorBackground, assigned above.
371		ColorSeverityLow = applyColor(t.SeverityLow, ColorDim)
372		ColorSeverityLowFg = applyColor(t.SeverityLowFg, ColorBackground)
373		ColorSeverityInfo = applyColor(t.SeverityInfo, ColorSeverityInfo)
374		ColorSeverityInfoFg = applyColor(t.SeverityInfoFg, ColorText)
375	
376		// Footer message colours (Rule 128). Assigned after the severity block
377		// because they alias it — the intent is that a footer error reads like a
378		// CRITICAL finding and a warning like a MEDIUM one.
379		ColorFooterInfo = ColorText
380		ColorFooterWarn = ColorSeverityMedium
381		ColorFooterError = ColorSeverityCritical
382		ColorInvalidField = ColorFooterError
383	
384		// Activity indicator colours (DEVDESK-137). Closed aliases, no theme key:
385		// running follows the structural colour, suspended and failed follow the
386		// footer warning and error levels assigned just above.
387		ColorActivityRunning = ColorSecondary
388		ColorActivityNeutral = ColorText
389		ColorActivitySuspended = ColorFooterWarn
390		ColorActivityFailed = ColorFooterError
391	
392		// The image update arrow (§3.88), in the structural colour: news, not a
393		// finding.
394		ColorUpdateAvailable = ColorSecondary
395	
396		// Icon colours (iconcolors.go). Assigned here like every other alias, and
397		// through applyColor so a theme file can name its own.
398		//
399		// The defaults carry an argument each. A namespace takes the structural
400		// colour the headers and tabs already use, and a repository the leaf colour
401		// beside it. Public is green because it is the state worth spotting without
402		// reading; internal is the warning hue because it is restricted without being
403		// closed; and private is **dim** because it is the majority — a colour every
404		// row carries informs of nothing (Rule 122), which is the same argument the
405		// severity counters make for their zeroes.
406		ColorIconNamespace = applyColor(t.IconNamespace, ColorSecondary)
407		ColorIconRepository = applyColor(t.IconRepository, ColorPrimary)
408		ColorIconVisPublic = applyColor(t.IconVisPublic, ColorOK)
409		ColorIconVisInternal = applyColor(t.IconVisInternal, ColorWarn)
410		ColorIconVisPrivate = applyColor(t.IconVisPrivate, ColorDim)
411	
412		// The workspaces and :sec listings. A directory takes the namespace's
413		// colour and the argument is the same shape: both are the thing that
414		// *holds* repositories, on a forge and on a disk. They are two roles rather
415		// than one alias so a theme can separate them; the default says they are
416		// the same idea.
417		ColorIconDirectory = applyColor(t.IconDirectory, ColorSecondary)
418	
419		// A loose file in a workspaces listing is the row nothing applies to — W, S
420		// and F are all greyed for it (Rule 130, availability.go). Dim is what the
421		// shortcut column already says about that row, said once more.
422		ColorIconFile = applyColor(t.IconFile, ColorDim)
423	
424		// An image takes the highlight rather than a third purple: Primary and
425		// Secondary are a mauve and a lavender one notch apart, and the :sec
426		// inventory's first column has exactly two values — the one place where the
427		// two would sit on adjacent rows with nothing else to separate them.
428		ColorIconImage = applyColor(t.IconImage, ColorHighlight)
429		// A container at rest is the nominal state, so its icon is plain text.
430		ColorIconContainer = applyColor(t.IconContainer, ColorText)
431	
432		// Token-mix bar (tokencolors.go). The fallbacks serve a user theme written
433		// before these keys existed; every shipped theme declares all four.
434		ColorTokenInput = applyColor(t.TokenInput, ColorSecondary)

300			Bold(true)
301	
302		s.Selected = s.Selected.
303			Background(ColorTableLineSelected).
304			Bold(true)
305	
306		return s
307	}

309	// TableStylesForState returns table styles with selection color based on row state.
310	// Use "error" for exited/dead containers, "normal" for default selection.
311	func TableStylesForState(state string) table.Styles {
312		s := DefaultTableStyles()
313		switch state {
314		case "error":
315			s.Selected = s.Selected.
316				Background(ColorError).
317				Foreground(ColorBlack)
318		case "busy":
319			// A row an action is running on. It outranks "error" rather than the
320			// other way round: `exited` is precisely what is about to stop being
321			// true, so the transition is the newer fact.
322			//
323			// ColorHighlight is not an arbitrary pick — the containers view already
324			// paints docker's own transitional states (`created`, `restarting`) with
325			// it, and a transition DevDesk started is the same kind of thing.
326			s.Selected = s.Selected.
327				Background(ColorHighlight).
328				Foreground(ColorBlack)
329		default:
330			// normal — uses DefaultTableStyles values (ColorSecondary bg, ColorBlack fg)
331		}
332		return s
333	}

335	// CertStateStyle colours a certificate state (status.CertState, passed as its
336	// string like StatusStyle and SeverityTextStyle take theirs — the theme
337	// package doesn't know about domain packages).
338	//
339	// It is kept separate from StatusStyle because the two vocabularies don't
340	// overlap: `to renew` has no StatusType of its own, and `expired` shares one
341	// with `error`. That is exactly what the Health box used to conflate.
342	//
343	// Orange is carried only by `to renew`: it's the only state that demands an
344	// action and still leaves time to take it.
345	func CertStateStyle(state string) lipgloss.Style {
346		switch state {
347		case "valid":
348			return StatusOKStyle
349		case "to renew":
350			return StatusWarningStyle
351		case "expired", "error":
352			return StatusErrorStyle
353		default:
354			return lipgloss.NewStyle().Background(ColorBackground)
355		}
356	}
357	
358	// CertStateIcon is the glyph that names a certificate state. All four have a
359	// distinct one — that's what was missing when `expired` and `error` shared
360	// the alert icon — and the hourglass says a renewal is coming, where the
361	// cross would say it's already too late.
362	func CertStateIcon(state string) string {
363		switch state {
364		case "valid":
365			return IconOK
366		case "to renew":
367			return IconHourglass
368		case "expired":
369			return IconError
370		case "error":
371			return IconWarning
372		default:
373			return IconWarning
374		}
375	}

377	// SeverityTextStyle returns the text style for a CVE severity, drawn from the
378	// same palette TableStylesForSeverity uses for the selected row. Callers pass
379	// the severity uppercased, as the scanners report it.
380	//
381	// Composing this by hand is what let the security details view render CRITICAL
382	// and HIGH identically (D11 in the backlog): ColorError + Bold happens to equal
383	// StatusErrorStyle, so the two collapsed.
384	func SeverityTextStyle(severity string) lipgloss.Style {
385		base := lipgloss.NewStyle().Background(ColorBackground)
386		switch strings.ToUpper(severity) {
387		case "CRITICAL":
388			return base.Foreground(ColorSeverityCritical).Bold(true)
389		case "HIGH":
390			return base.Foreground(ColorSeverityHigh).Bold(true)
391		case "MEDIUM":
392			return base.Foreground(ColorSeverityMedium)
393		case "LOW":
394			return base.Foreground(ColorSeverityLow)
395		default:
396			return base.Foreground(ColorSeverityInfo)
397		}
398	}

154	// ThemeDir returns the themes directory (~/.devdesk/themes/)
155	func ThemeDir() (string, error) {
156		homeDir, err := os.UserHomeDir()
157		if err != nil {
158			return "", err
159		}
160		return filepath.Join(homeDir, ".devdesk", "themes"), nil
161	}

163	// LoadTheme loads a theme from a JSON file.
164	// If name is empty, "dark" or "default", returns the built-in default theme
165	func LoadTheme(name string) (*Theme, error) {
166		if name == "" || name == "dark" || name == "default" {
167			return DefaultTheme(), nil
168		}
169	
170		data, err := readThemeFile(name)
171		if err != nil {
172			return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to read theme '%s': %w", name, err)
173		}
174	
175		var t Theme
176		if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &t); err != nil {
177			return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to parse theme '%s': %w", name, err)
178		}
179	
180		if err := validateTheme(&t); err != nil {
181			return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid theme '%s': %w", name, err)
182		}
183	
184		// Ensure the name is set
185		if t.Name == "" {
186			t.Name = name
187		}
188	
189		return &t, nil
190	}

192	// readThemeFile returns the bytes of <name>.json: the user's copy in
193	// ~/.devdesk/themes first, then the one embedded in the binary. A name that is
194	// in neither gives an error wrapping fs.ErrNotExist.
195	func readThemeFile(name string) ([]byte, error) {
196		file := name + ".json"
197		if dir, err := ThemeDir(); err == nil {
198			data, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(dir, file))
199			if err == nil || !errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist) {
200				return data, err
201			}
202		}
203		return themes.FS.ReadFile(file)
204	}

206	// ListThemes returns the list of available themes: "default" (built-in) first,
207	// then the union of the shipped themes and the JSON files in the themes
208	// directory, sorted, without duplicates.
209	func ListThemes() ([]string, error) {
210		seen := map[string]bool{"default": true}
211		var names []string
212		add := func(entries []fs.DirEntry) {
213			for _, entry := range entries {
214				if entry.IsDir() {
215					continue
216				}
217				if themeName, ok := strings.CutSuffix(entry.Name(), ".json"); ok && !seen[themeName] {
218					seen[themeName] = true
219					names = append(names, themeName)
220				}
221			}
222		}
223		if dir, err := ThemeDir(); err == nil {
224			if entries, err := os.ReadDir(dir); err == nil {
225				add(entries)
226			}
227		}
228		if entries, err := themes.FS.ReadDir("."); err == nil {
229			add(entries)
230		}
231		sort.Strings(names)
232		return append([]string{"default"}, names...), nil
233	}

235	// hexColorPattern is the only colour form a theme file may hold.
236	var hexColorPattern = regexp.MustCompile(`^#([0-9a-fA-F]{3}|[0-9a-fA-F]{6})$`)

238	// validateTheme treats every string field of Theme other than name as a colour
239	// (a new non-colour string field must be excluded here). It refuses a theme
240	// holding a non-empty colour that is not #rgb or #rrggbb, naming the first
241	// such key (in declaration order) and its value. An empty value is not an error:
242	// it selects the fallback applyColor documents.
243	func validateTheme(t *Theme) error {
244		v := reflect.ValueOf(t).Elem()
245		for i := 0; i < v.NumField(); i++ {
246			key, _, _ := strings.Cut(v.Type().Field(i).Tag.Get("json"), ",")
247			if key == "name" || v.Field(i).Kind() != reflect.String {
248				continue
249			}
250			if val := v.Field(i).String(); val != "" && !hexColorPattern.MatchString(val) {
251				return fmt.Errorf("%s: %q is not #rgb or #rrggbb", key, val)
252			}
253		}
254		return nil
255	}

257	// applyColor returns a color.Color from a hex string, or the fallback if empty.
258	func applyColor(hex string, fallback color.Color) color.Color {
259		if hex == "" {

261		}
262		return lipgloss.Color(hex)
263	}

265	// Hex formats c as "#rrggbb". Anything that is not a color.RGBA (NoColor, the
266	// empty Color, an ANSI index, nil) has no fixed value and gives "none".
267	func Hex(c color.Color) string {
268		rgb, err := rgb8(c, "hex")
269		if err != nil {
270			return "none"
271		}
272		return fmt.Sprintf("#%02x%02x%02x", rgb[0], rgb[1], rgb[2])
273	}

276	// then refreshing all styles

290		ColorBlack = lipgloss.Color(t.ColorBlack)
291		ColorBackground = applyColor(t.ColorBackground, ColorBackground)
292	
293		// Apply per-component colors (falling back to semantic colors)
294		ColorTitleFg = applyColor(t.TitleFg, ColorPrimary)
295		ColorAppTitleFg = applyColor(t.AppTitleFg, ColorPrimary)
296		ColorSubTitleFg = applyColor(t.SubTitleFg, ColorSecondary)
297	
298		ColorButtonFg = applyColor(t.ButtonFg, ColorWhite)
299		ColorButtonBg = applyColor(t.ButtonBg, ColorPrimary)

302	
303		ColorTabActiveFg = applyColor(t.TabActiveFg, ColorBlack)
304		ColorTabActiveBg = applyColor(t.TabActiveBg, ColorSecondary)

306		ColorTabInactiveBg = applyColor(t.TabInactiveBg, ColorCmdLineBg)
307

309	
310		ColorCmdLineFg = applyColor(t.CmdLineFg, ColorHighlight)
311		ColorCmdLineBg = applyColor(t.CmdLineBg, ColorCmdLineBg)
312	
313		// Falls back to ColorCmdLineBg: assigned after ColorCmdLineBg above rather
314		// than beside the other Table* colors, since a fallback read before
315		// ColorCmdLineBg's own assignment this pass would see last theme's value
316		// instead of this one's, the same ordering ColorChartBg below depends on.
317		// Any theme file predating this key omits it, so this fallback is what most
318		// installs actually render with.
319		ColorTableLineSelected = applyColor(t.TableLineSelected, ColorCmdLineBg)
320	
321		// A chart's background is that of the command line: it's the surface

326		ColorCmdLineInactiveFg = applyColor(t.CmdLineInactiveFg, ColorDim)

332		// Syntax colors: aliases of the semantic palette, assigned here rather than
333		// at declaration because the palette itself is only populated by this
334		// function — a package-level `= ColorSecondary` would capture the zero
335		// value and never follow a theme change. ColorChartBg above is the same
336		// pattern.
337		ColorSyntaxKey = ColorSecondary
338		ColorSyntaxString = ColorOK
339		ColorSyntaxNumber = ColorHighlight
340		ColorSyntaxLiteral = ColorPrimary
341		ColorSyntaxPunct = ColorDim
342		ColorSyntaxTag = ColorSecondary
343		ColorSyntaxAttr = ColorPrimary
344		ColorSyntaxComment = ColorDim
345	
346		// A keyword shares the literal's colour today, and that is deliberate
347		// rather than an oversight: `if` and `true` are both words of the language,
348		// so the pairing is defensible until a theme decides otherwise — at which
349		// point it has a name to decide about. It is the argument already made for
350		// ColorFooterError against ColorError.
351		ColorSyntaxKeyword = ColorPrimary
352	
353		// A heading takes the key colour, and its weight comes from the style
354		// rather than from here.
355		ColorSyntaxHeading = ColorSecondary
356	
357		ColorSearchMatch = ColorHighlight
358		ColorSearchMatchFg = ColorBlack
359	
360		// Severity colors (background + foreground pairs)

362		ColorSeverityCriticalFg = applyColor(t.SeverityCriticalFg, ColorBlack)
363		ColorSeverityHigh = applyColor(t.SeverityHigh, ColorSeverityHigh)
364		ColorSeverityHighFg = applyColor(t.SeverityHighFg, ColorBlack)
365		ColorSeverityMedium = applyColor(t.SeverityMedium, ColorWarn)
366		ColorSeverityMediumFg = applyColor(t.SeverityMediumFg, ColorBlack)
367		// A theme that omits the two LOW keys gets ColorDim under ColorBackground,
368		// the pair the shipped dark themes set (D181). ColorDim is held to 4.5:1 on
369		// the background on every theme, so the pair reads on dark and light alike.
370		// Both fallbacks read ColorDim and ColorBackground, assigned above.
371		ColorSeverityLow = applyColor(t.SeverityLow, ColorDim)
372		ColorSeverityLowFg = applyColor(t.SeverityLowFg, ColorBackground)
373		ColorSeverityInfo = applyColor(t.SeverityInfo, ColorSeverityInfo)
374		ColorSeverityInfoFg = applyColor(t.SeverityInfoFg, ColorText)
375	
376		// Footer message colours (Rule 128). Assigned after the severity block
377		// because they alias it — the intent is that a footer error reads like a
378		// CRITICAL finding and a warning like a MEDIUM one.
379		ColorFooterInfo = ColorText
380		ColorFooterWarn = ColorSeverityMedium
381		ColorFooterError = ColorSeverityCritical
382		ColorInvalidField = ColorFooterError

384		// Activity indicator colours (DEVDESK-137). Closed aliases, no theme key:
385		// running follows the structural colour, suspended and failed follow the

389		ColorActivitySuspended = ColorFooterWarn

391	
392		// The image update arrow (§3.88), in the structural colour: news, not a

396		// Icon colours (iconcolors.go). Assigned here like every other alias, and

408		ColorIconVisPublic = applyColor(t.IconVisPublic, ColorOK)
409		ColorIconVisInternal = applyColor(t.IconVisInternal, ColorWarn)
410		ColorIconVisPrivate = applyColor(t.IconVisPrivate, ColorDim)

412		// The workspaces and :sec listings. A directory takes the namespace's

417		ColorIconDirectory = applyColor(t.IconDirectory, ColorSecondary)

419		// A loose file in a workspaces listing is the row nothing applies to — W, S

422		ColorIconFile = applyColor(t.IconFile, ColorDim)

428		ColorIconImage = applyColor(t.IconImage, ColorHighlight)

430		ColorIconContainer = applyColor(t.IconContainer, ColorText)
431	
432		// Token-mix bar (tokencolors.go). The fallbacks serve a user theme written
433		// before these keys existed; every shipped theme declares all four.
434		ColorTokenInput = applyColor(t.TokenInput, ColorSecondary)

309	// TableStylesForState returns table styles with selection color based on row state.
310	// Use "error" for exited/dead containers, "normal" for default selection.
311	func TableStylesForState(state string) table.Styles {
312		s := DefaultTableStyles()
313		switch state {
314		case "error":
315			s.Selected = s.Selected.
316				Background(ColorError).
317				Foreground(ColorBlack)
318		case "busy":
319			// A row an action is running on. It outranks "error" rather than the
320			// other way round: `exited` is precisely what is about to stop being
321			// true, so the transition is the newer fact.
322			//
323			// ColorHighlight is not an arbitrary pick — the containers view already
324			// paints docker's own transitional states (`created`, `restarting`) with
325			// it, and a transition DevDesk started is the same kind of thing.
326			s.Selected = s.Selected.
327				Background(ColorHighlight).
328				Foreground(ColorBlack)
329		default:
330			// normal — uses DefaultTableStyles values (ColorSecondary bg, ColorBlack fg)
331		}
332		return s
333	}
334	
335	// CertStateStyle colours a certificate state (status.CertState, passed as its
336	// string like StatusStyle and SeverityTextStyle take theirs — the theme
337	// package doesn't know about domain packages).
338	//
339	// It is kept separate from StatusStyle because the two vocabularies don't
340	// overlap: `to renew` has no StatusType of its own, and `expired` shares one
341	// with `error`. That is exactly what the Health box used to conflate.
342	//
343	// Orange is carried only by `to renew`: it's the only state that demands an
344	// action and still leaves time to take it.
345	func CertStateStyle(state string) lipgloss.Style {
346		switch state {
347		case "valid":
348			return StatusOKStyle
349		case "to renew":
350			return StatusWarningStyle
351		case "expired", "error":
352			return StatusErrorStyle
353		default:
354			return lipgloss.NewStyle().Background(ColorBackground)
355		}
356	}
357	
358	// CertStateIcon is the glyph that names a certificate state. All four have a
359	// distinct one — that's what was missing when `expired` and `error` shared
360	// the alert icon — and the hourglass says a renewal is coming, where the
361	// cross would say it's already too late.
362	func CertStateIcon(state string) string {
363		switch state {
364		case "valid":
365			return IconOK
366		case "to renew":
367			return IconHourglass
368		case "expired":
369			return IconError
370		case "error":
371			return IconWarning
372		default:
373			return IconWarning
374		}
375	}
376	
377	// SeverityTextStyle returns the text style for a CVE severity, drawn from the
378	// same palette TableStylesForSeverity uses for the selected row. Callers pass
379	// the severity uppercased, as the scanners report it.
380	//
381	// Composing this by hand is what let the security details view render CRITICAL
382	// and HIGH identically (D11 in the backlog): ColorError + Bold happens to equal
383	// StatusErrorStyle, so the two collapsed.
384	func SeverityTextStyle(severity string) lipgloss.Style {
385		base := lipgloss.NewStyle().Background(ColorBackground)
386		switch strings.ToUpper(severity) {
387		case "CRITICAL":
388			return base.Foreground(ColorSeverityCritical).Bold(true)
389		case "HIGH":
390			return base.Foreground(ColorSeverityHigh).Bold(true)
391		case "MEDIUM":
392			return base.Foreground(ColorSeverityMedium)
393		case "LOW":
394			return base.Foreground(ColorSeverityLow)
395		default:
396			return base.Foreground(ColorSeverityInfo)
397		}
398	}

401	func TableStylesForSeverity(severity string) table.Styles {

407				Foreground(ColorSeverityCriticalFg)
408		case "HIGH":

410				Background(ColorSeverityHigh).
411				Foreground(ColorSeverityHighFg)
412		case "MEDIUM":
413			s.Selected = s.Selected.
414				Background(ColorSeverityMedium).
415				Foreground(ColorSeverityMediumFg)
416		case "LOW":
417			s.Selected = s.Selected.
418				Background(ColorSeverityLow).
419				Foreground(ColorSeverityLowFg)
420		case "UNKNOWN", "INFO":

422				Background(ColorSeverityInfo).
423				Foreground(ColorSeverityInfoFg)
424		default:
425			// normal — uses DefaultTableStyles values
426		}

# Text contrast, part B of DEVDESK-770: the severity badges and the gauge rail

Measurement note of 2026-11-24. It follows `2026-11-24-theme-text-contrast.md` and `2026-11-24-theme-text-contrast-2.md`,
which are frozen: the second one lists the LOW and HIGH badges and the gauge rail under "Not done here", and this note
is what closes them. Nothing in those two notes is rewritten here. The decision is D181 in `docs/backlog.md`.

| | |
|---|---|
| Method | `theme.ContrastRatio(foreground, surface)` and `theme.ColorDistance` (CIE76 delta E), after `ApplyTheme(DefaultTheme())` then `ApplyTheme(<theme>)` for the default theme and each file of `themes/*.json`, read by a throwaway test (deleted) run on the commit before this change (themes read with `git show HEAD:themes/<name>.json`; for `default`, the old LOW pair `#585b70` / `#cdd6f4`) and on this one. The guards that hold the result are `TestEverySeverityBadgeReachesTextContrastOnEveryTheme`, `TestSeverityBadgeTextIsTheAppBackgroundOnEveryTheme`, `TestSeverityHighAndCriticalStayApart` (threshold 8), `TestEveryTextColourReachesItsContrastOnEveryTheme` (`ColorSeverityHigh` and `ColorSeverityLow`), `REDACTED` and `TestTheGaugeTrackIsTheViewportBorderOnEveryTheme` |
| Thresholds | 4.5:1 for the badge text on the badge, and for the badge colour on the background when it is painted as text (WCAG 1.4.3); 3:1 for the badge colour on the selected row (a glyph, Rule 118); CIE76 delta E of at least 8 between CRITICAL and HIGH. No ratio is held for the rail |
| Retuning rule | HIGH: same hue and same HSL saturation, lightness moved by steps of 0.005 away from the surfaces, by the smallest step (`minimalToneFor`, `tune_test.go`). LOW: `severity_low` is `color_dim` (already held to 4.5:1). The text of every badge is `color_background`. Tokens: same hue, lightness and saturation moved to the nearest colour (smallest delta E) that holds every guard of `tokencolors_test.go` |
| Themes | the 13 shipped ones. `default` and `catppuccin-mocha` are the same palette |

## What changed

| Key | Themes | Moves |
|---|---|---|
| `severity_high` | latte, one-dark, solarized-dark, nord, solarized-light | raised to 4.5:1 for the badge text |
| `severity_low` | the eight dark themes (frappe, macchiato, mocha, dark-plus, nord, one-dark, solarized-dark, tokyo-night) and `default` | set to `color_dim` (github-dark already was; the three light themes already held) |
| `severity_low_fg` | all 13 | set to `color_background` |
| `GaugeTrackStyle` | all 13 | `ColorSeverityLow` becomes `ColorViewportBorder` |
| `token_cache_read` / `token_input` | latte, github-light, solarized-light / nord | moved off the new rail tone |
| fallbacks in `ApplyTheme` | a theme that omits the LOW keys | `ColorCmdLineBg` and `ColorText` become `ColorDim` and `ColorBackground` |

Before this change, 5 of 13 themes had a HIGH badge under 4.5:1 (latte 3.48, one-dark 2.95, solarized-dark 3.26,
nord 4.39, solarized-light 4.27), and 10 of 13 a LOW badge under it (from 1.21 on solarized-light to 4.17 on
macchiato). After it, none of the four badges is under 4.5:1 on any theme; the lowest text-on-badge ratios are nord HIGH
and dark-plus LOW, both 4.52.

Amends points 3 and 4 of D177. Decided (orchestrator, 2026-11-24, within the autonomy the user granted; the user can overrule).**

101	**D181 — DEVDESK-770 part B: the severity badges reach 4.5:1 on the 13 themes, with their text set to the application background, and the gauge rail goes back to the frame border. Amends points 3 and 4 of D177. Decided (orchestrator, 2026-11-24, within the autonomy the user granted; the user can overrule).**
102	
103	1. **Decided, HIGH.** `severity_high` is raised on five themes (latte `#e64553` to `#d61d2d`, one-dark `#be5046` to `#cf7d75`, solarized-dark `#cb4b16` to `#e8652e`, nord `#d08770` to `#d18a74`, solarized-light `#cb4b16` to `#c44815`), by the smallest lightness step (same hue and HSL saturation) that reaches 4.5:1 for the badge text on it. The other eight already held. CRITICAL and HIGH keep a CIE76 distance of at least 8 on every theme (`TestSeverityHighAndCriticalStayApart`); the closest pair stays macchiato at 8.9, latte moves from 11.7 to 9.0.
104	2. **Decided, LOW.** `severity_low` is `color_dim` on every dark theme (eight change, github-dark already was) and on the default theme (`#585b70` to `#979aad`). The LOW badge becomes a light badge with dark text, like HIGH, instead of a dark badge with light text that missed 4.5:1 on 10 of 13 themes (1.2 to 4.2). On the three light themes and github-dark `severity_low` already held and does not move.
105	3. **Decided, the badge text.** `severity_*_fg` of CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM and LOW is `color_background` on every theme (`TestSeverityBadgeTextIsTheAppBackgroundOnEveryTheme`): a light badge carries dark text and a dark one light text, the foreground follows the theme's surface instead of a tone nobody holds to a ratio, and one number moves per badge. INFO and UNKNOWN keep their muted badge and are not decided here. The fallbacks of a theme that omits the LOW keys are `ColorDim` and `ColorBackground` (D177 had `ColorCmdLineBg` and `ColorText`, because `ColorDim` was then a light text tone under a light `ColorText`; both fallbacks now read on every theme since `ColorDim` is held to 4.5:1 on the background).
106	4. **Amends D177, point 3** ("the 13 shipped themes keep their own `severity_low`; the fallback is `ColorCmdLineBg`"): the shipped value is `color_dim` and the fallback is `ColorDim`. D177 point 2 (why `ColorSeverityLow` cannot follow `ColorDim` while the text on it stays light) is overtaken, not wrong: the text on it is no longer light. **Amends D177, point 4** ("the LOW badge foreground and the HIGH one stay under 4.5:1"): they reach it, `TestEverySeverityBadgeReachesTextContrastOnEveryTheme`.
107	5. **The gauge rail is the frame border again.** `GaugeTrackStyle()` is `ColorViewportBorder`, not `ColorSeverityLow` (§3.71 aliased it, then D177 kept the dark tone for it). With `ColorSeverityLow` at the tone of `ColorDim`, the track of every empty cell would be as bright as a label. The border is the tone the application already draws its lines in, and a rail is a line drawn inside the frame. **The cost, accepted and written here:** the border is held to 3:1 on the background (D179) but not on the selected row, where it is 2.2 to 2.8:1 on 11 of the 13 themes. The comparison with before (the rail, `ColorSeverityLow`, was 1.4 to 2.9:1 under the cursor on eight themes) covers only the themes that did not already reach 3:1; on four themes the rail gets worse: on the selected row it falls from 4.05 / 5.62 / 4.93 / 4.39:1 to 2.22 / 2.74 / 2.82 / 2.65:1 on latte / github-dark / github-light / solarized-light, from above 3:1 to below it (on the background, from 5.0 to 6.2:1 to 3.0, because the LOW tone was a text colour there). Under the cursor the rail is faint, and the number beside the gauge carries the value (the fill, the number and the glyph shape stay the carriers, Rule 122). A contrast ratio is not held for the rail, on purpose (`TestTheGaugeTrackIsTheViewportBorderOnEveryTheme` holds that it is the border, visible against the background and the selected row).
108	6. **Four token colours move.** The rail is now a tone `TestTokenColorsAreNotSeverityOrGaugeColours` (delta E 20 from the severity and gauge colours) keeps the token colours away from, and it caught four of them, which move by the smallest delta E, same hue, to the nearest tone that holds every other guard: latte `token_cache_read` `#607670` to `#5d746e` (delta E 1.0), github-light `token_cache_read` `#748db4` to `#6888bb` (7.3), nord `token_input` `#7b91bf` to `#7f9bd4` (7.0), solarized-light `token_cache_read` `#87836e` to `#878163` (5.3). The test is not loosened.
109	7. **A colour is never the only carrier of the level** (WCAG 1.4.1): the Severity cell spells the level out in full and never loses its column (`TestTheSeverityCellSpellsTheLevelOut`, `TestTheSeverityWordIsRenderedOnEveryRowAt80Columns`).
110	8. **Not decided here.** INFO and UNKNOWN, the `Yes` and success buttons, the error row (`ColorBlack` on `ColorError`, 3.05 on nord), and the severity counts of the inventory under the cursor, which stay at the 3:1 glyph threshold. Figures: `docs/measurements/2026-11-24-theme-text-contrast-3.md`.
111	
112	**D178 — DEVDESK-769: a breadcrumb trail that is too long for its line drops its head and cuts its current segment, through `theme.RenderTrail`; the pills stay. Decided (architect and user, 2026-11-24; the user can overrule).**
113	
114	1. **Defect.** The four breadcrumb rows (`ws`, the forge explorer, `:jobs`, the registry level of OCI resources) drew every pill with `PadWithBg(Bg(" ")+RenderTabs(...), width)`. Past the width the line overflowed, and the terminal wrapped it onto the next row.
115	2. **Decided.** The pills `" label "`, one cell apart, are kept. The current segment is always the last one. No "home" anchor is kept: when the trail does not fit, the head becomes one `…` pill and the largest tail that fits stays; if the current segment alone does not fit, it is cut at its end with `…`. Under 8 cells of room only the cut segment is drawn, under 3 nothing.
116	3. **Rejected.** Shrinking every label (no segment stays readable), keeping the first pill as an anchor (it costs cells the current segment needs), and a scrolling trail (a second navigation to learn on a row that is not navigable, Rule 123).
117	4. **Where.** `theme.FitTrail` and `theme.RenderTrail`; see `docs/architecture/ui-components.md`, "Breadcrumb trails that fit".
118	
119	**D179 — DEVDESK-770 part A: the frame border reaches 3:1 on all 13 shipped themes, a departure from the third-party palettes. Decided (user, 2026-11-24).**
120	
121	1. **Decided.** `ColorViewportBorder` reaches 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11, a non-text object) against `ColorBackground` on every shipped theme (`TestEveryTextColourReachesItsContrastOnEveryTheme`). It lightens on the dark themes and darkens on the light ones; `color_border` follows `viewport_border` (the same hex on every theme). Ten themes move (github-dark `#30363d` to `#56616e` and github-light `#d0d7de` to `#8597a9` the most, delta E 18.7 and 25.1); default, mocha and macchiato already held.
122	2. **Why it departs from the palettes.** The shipped border tones were below 3:1 on ten themes (1.69:1 on nord, 2.30:1 on latte). The other colours of this part (`ColorSecondary`, `ColorPrimary` and their followers, the active tab, the inactive buttons) are retuned as in DEVDESK-764: same hue and saturation, the smallest lightness step; `cmd_line_inactive_fg` is aligned on `color_dim` instead. Figures: `docs/measurements/2026-11-24-theme-text-contrast-2.md`.
123	3. **Not decided here.** The LOW and HIGH badges and the gauge rail (part B), the non-chromatic signal of secondary text on solarized and latte (out of scope by decision of the user), the `Yes` and success buttons, INFO and UNKNOWN: "Not done here" of that note. 
124	
125	**D180 — DEVDESK-767: the scan's renderers (kustomize, helm) run with the network cut. Decided (architect, 2026-11-24; the user can overrule).**
126	
127	1. **The hole.** A repository that is scanned is not trusted, and a `kustomization.yaml` that names `git@host:o/r` or `https://host/m.yaml` makes kustomize fetch it, with the user's ssh agent, proxy and credentials, before anything was validated. DEVDESK-763 closed the folder name; this closes the content.
128	2. **Decided.** helm and kustomize run offline: from a binary with `offlineEnviron` (host proxy variables, `REQUEST_METHOD`, `GIT_ALLOW_PROTOCOL`, `LC_ALL`, `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `GIT_SSH*`, `GIT_PROXY_COMMAND` and `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT` removed; `GIT_ALLOW_PROTOCOL=devdesk-none` (no transport, so `file://` is refused too), `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`, a dead proxy `http://127.0.0.1:0`, `NO_PROXY=` and `LC_ALL=C` added), from an image with `containerRun.Offline` (`--network none`, no proxy forwarded). kubeconform keeps its network (it downloads schemas). Rejected: a name or URL filter on the overlay (the format is open: git URLs, go-getter, ssh), and one switch for the whole scan.
129	3. **The way out.** `scan.tools.kustomize.allow_remote_bases` (default false, `omitempty`; checkbox "Allow remote bases" in the configuration view) gives kustomize its network back, for a repository the user trusts. helm has no such key: it reads no remote base.
130	4. **A refused fetch is its own finding**, `Overlay does not build: remote base blocked` (K8S-RENDER, HIGH, whole message kept), recognised by `remoteBlocked` and only when the run was offline. Rejected: leaving kustomize's raw message, which reads as a broken overlay.
131	5. **Limits and risks.** Native markers measured on kustomize v5.8.3 and git 2.47.3; the container markers (`no such host`, `Could not resolve host`, `network is unreachable`, `no 'git' program`) are expected and not measured, no engine was reachable; Windows not measured. A native base on the loopback still gets a GET (Go never applies a proxy to the loopback). The scan cache serves an old result until the next rescan. `--dependency-update` in `scan.tools.helm.args` now fails: vendor the dependency in `charts/`.
132	6. **Not decided here.** No ADR: reversible by a revert, one `omitempty` key, no cache schema change. **Plane:** DEVDESK-767. Number: D177 is the highest in this worktree; re-check at merge. Sources: `internal/scan/render_network.go`, `internal/scan/container_run.go`, `internal/scan/kubeconform_render.go`, `internal/config/scan_tools.go`, `docs/architecture/scanning.md`, `docs/architecture/network.md`, `docs/architecture/configuration.md`.**
133	
134	**D177 — DEVDESK-764: `severity_low` no longer takes the tone of `ColorDim`; it keeps the darker tone it had before. Replaces the decision of §3.73 ("`severity_low` prend le ton de `ColorDim`"). Decided (orchestrator, 2026-11-24, after the review of DEVDESK-764; the user can overrule).**
135	
136	1. **Replaced decision.** §3.73 made the default of `severity_low` equal to `color_dim` (`#585b70` on the default theme), and made the fallback of `ColorSeverityLow` in `ApplyTheme` `ColorDim`, so that a LOW finding read like a "0" count in the `:sec` inventory.
137	2. **Why it no longer holds.** DEVDESK-764 raised `ColorDim` to 4.5:1 as a text colour on every shipped theme (default `#585b70` to `#979aad`), so it is now a light tone. `ColorSeverityLow` is also the background of the LOW badge, under `ColorSeverityLowFg` (`ColorText` by default): following `ColorDim` would put a light text on a light badge (about 2:1).
138	3. **Decided.** The 13 shipped themes keep their own `severity_low` (the old dim tone). The fallback of `ColorSeverityLow` for a theme that omits the key is `ColorCmdLineBg` again (the value from before §3.73), so that the `ColorText` fallback of `severity_low_fg` stays readable (`TestAThemeWithoutSeverityLowKeepsAReadableLowBadge`). A "0" count in `:sec` still uses `DimStyle`; the two keys are separate, as §3.73 already allowed.
139	4. **Not decided here.** The LOW badge foreground (1.2 to 3.6:1) and the HIGH one (one-dark, solarized-dark, latte) stay under 4.5:1: listed under "Not done here" in `docs/measurements/2026-11-24-theme-text-contrast.md`.
